title: Again, this is only focusing on live productions I saw! Not counting ...
transcript: I did it, folks! I have now seen a live production of every single Shakespeare play! So in honor of completing one of my biggest lifelong bucket list challenges, I'm gonna do a Shakespeare Wrapped! To start with, a little overview and a brief note on what I'm counting and what I'm not. We have 38 plays we're talking about here. I am, including two noble kinsmen, not including Edward III. Fight me on that in the comments if you wish, but this is my list. and I've seen those 38 plays over the course of 120 different productions, not counting, I think, three repeats of seeing the same production twice. Likewise, there's a lot of gray area and subjectivity of like, where's the line between a production and an adaptation? How do you count like, mashups, double bills, two part productions, etc? I would bore you if I got into the details, but suffice it to say I made a lot of case by case judgment calls. And just for fun, I separately tallied up the full-on adaptations. Things like West Side Story, Fat Ham. Although 15 seems low, I think I might have forgotten some. Likewise, I separately tallied up shows that were otherwise inspired by Shakespeare's plays, sequels, spin offs, etc. And again, just for fun, 3 shows where Will Shakespeare himself is a character. But the rest of these stats are just gonna do with those 38 plays and those 120 productions. here on the left, we can see the plays that I've seen performed live the most. Romeo and Juliet topping the list with 11. Hamlet also at 11, but one of those was a repeat Twelfth Night at 7.5 because I did leave one production at intermission. And shockingly, Winter's Tale in sixth. And on the right you can see the list of plays that I have only ever seen performed live one time. I've seen Shakespeare performed in six different languages: English, Dutch, German, Japanese, Greek, and Russian, as well as two primarily English language productions that strategically translated some segments into other languages, one in Spanish and one in Farsi. Here's a breakdown by genre for all of the different productions that I've seen. So 39.2% tragedy, 28% comedy, 16% history, and 16.8% the other ones that were still not sure how to categorize. Here's a breakdown by location. Almost 61% of all Shakespeare productions I've seen were in New York, Almost 22% were in London, plus another 2.5% in Stratford upon Avon, and the rest divided up between the Bay Area, where I'm from, Ashland, Oregon, where they have the Oregon Shakespeare Festival. We have the productions I saw on my college campus in Yonkers, New York, plus one production in Athens, Greece. Here we have kind of the scale of the production or how high profile it was. We have 62.5% that I would categorize as a major production. Although I was pretty liberal with this, I included a lot of Off Broadway companies in here, then we have 13% in like mid-sized companies, 15% as smaller, more low budget indie productions and 9% amateur productions. Maybe surprising or maybe not, We have a whopping 28% of all Shakespeare productions I've seen that were performed outdoors. And finally, here is a timeline of when I crossed each play off my list. The first Shakespeare play I ever saw in 2009 was Romeo and Juliet. I crossed a bunch of them off my list in 2016 and 2017. That was when I was really seeing a lot more Shakespeare. Plus I was studying abroad in London. Made some more good progress in 2023. And then the last couple years I have been really crawling to that finish line. Of course, I have to give a shout out to Armorica Theatre Company for doing Two Gentlemen of Verona, allowing me to cross the last one off my list today.
classificationReason: A 'Shakespeare Wrapped' retrospective covering all 38 Shakespeare plays across 120 productions. Classic roundup with no single show as the primary focus.
